catalog_quote: 1.2.3. El Acento. El acento principal aparece con más frecuencia en la sílaba penúltima o antepenúltima del grupo intensivo. Cae en la última, sólo en el vocativo enfático, como en /iná/ '¡mamá!'. En esta posición está acompañado de una prolongación notable y de un cambio y disminución del tono. Muchas veces, también, la sílaba que precede a la antepenúltima, es la que recibe el acento principal cuando está formada por el primer miembro de una combinación de vocales. Por otro lado, existen pocas palabras con acento en la sílaba indicada: /pishimáatakye/ 'estás pescando con flecha'. [p.9, sec. 1.1.3:] El acento. Ej.: /paníro/ 'su sobrina (de usted)' y /pániro/ 'uno'; /samáni/ 'majás' y /sámani/ 'lejos'; /ikyianakyéro/ 'él está entrando' y /ikyianákyero/ 'él la está llevando en sus espaldas'.
new_statements.translation: 1.2.3. Stress. Primary stress appears most frequently on the penultimate or antepenultimate syllable of the stress group. It falls on the final syllable only in the emphatic vocative, as in /iná/ 'mother!'. [...] Often, too, the syllable preceding the antepenult is the one that receives primary stress when it consists of the first member of a vowel sequence. [p.9, 1.1.3:] Stress. The existence of a phonemic stress is demonstrated by several word pairs, e.g. /paníro/ 'your niece' vs /pániro/ 'one'; /samáni/ 'paca' vs /sámani/ 'far'; /ikyianakyéro/ 'he is entering' vs /ikyianákyero/ 'he is carrying her on his back'.

I re-rendered pp.3-5, 9, 11 and 33 with page render (no scanned) and read them directly. p.11, sec. 1.2.3 'El Acento': 'El acento principal aparece con mas frecuencia en la silaba penultima o antepenultima del grupo intensivo. Cae en la ultima, solo en el vocativo enfatico, como en /ina/ !mama!. En esta posicion esta acompanado de una prolongacion notable y de un cambio y disminucion del tono. Muchas veces, tambien, la silaba que precede a la antepenultima, es la que recibe el acento principal…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Snell treats stress as phonemic (a 'fonema de acento', with minimal pairs) but confined to a right-edge window: primary stress falls on the penult or antepenult of the stress group ('grupo intensivo'), never on the final syllable except in emphatic vocatives, and sometimes on the pre-antepenult when that syllable is the first vowel of a vowel sequence. Her later dictionaries (1998/2008 p.14; 2011 p.18) operationalise this as: penultimate stress is the unmarked default and antepenultimate stress is lexically marked with a written accent on headwords (pánkotsi vs tinti, punatagantsi). A native-speaker pedagogical grammar (Chineri et al. 2020 pp.224-226) adds that antepenult stress is very frequent and partly conditioned by vowel quality (weak penult e/i with strong antepenult a/o/u) and morphology (imperatives, -rika/-mera/-rira, many -empa reflexives), suggesting a sonority-sensitive system like closely related Nanti; no formal metrical analysis of Matsigenka itself was found.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Snell 1978 p.9: 'También aparecen acentos secundarios, los cuales, en nuestro análisis, hasta el presente, no se consideran según la colocación del acento principal' — secondary stresses exist but were left unanalysed (note 8 p.33 calls for further study of stress definition/distribution and its relation to rhythm groups).
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress only in emphatic vocative (iná), with lengthening and pitch change; pre-antepenult stress when it is V1 of a vowel cluster; a few words like pishimáatakye; under agitation/emphasis stress shifts antepenult->penult, sometimes with vowel doubling (néro ~ neéro/nehéro; poreatsíri ~ poreátsiri); note 9: primary stress never on /i/ as second member of a vowel cluster nor on the second of two identical vowels (except where root-initial /h/ is dropped: noíme ~ nohíme), /e/ of /ae/ never stressed; stressed vowels often lengthened, high pitch on the stressed syllable in isolation; Snell 2011: stress unpredictable in onomatopoeic words and variable in descriptive particles; Snell 2011 glosses the contrast as 'acento (o acento tonal)'.
new_statements.domain_note: Snell's domain is the 'grupo intensivo' (stress group of 2-20 syllables bounded by potential pause, exactly one primary stress) rather than the grammatical word; dictionary citation forms follow the penult-default/antepenult-marked convention. Data from Urubamba-area Matsigenka (materials gathered from 1952 on; dictionary distinguishes Alto vs Bajo Urubamba).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Urubamba-area Machiguenga/Matsigenka = mach1267 (Snell's informants Alto/Bajo Urubamba; Snell 1978 notes Solís 1973 described a different dialect). Nanti (nant1250), analysed by Crowhurst & Michael 2005 / Michael 2008, is a separate Glottolog language and was used only as comparative context.

sources.citation: Snell, Betty A. (comp.); Mary Ruth Wise (ed.). 2011. Diccionario matsigenka—castellano con índice castellano, notas enciclopédicas y apuntes gramaticales. Serie Lingüística Peruana 56. Lima: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano. 895 pp.
sources.note: 'Alfabeto y pronunciación', p.18 'El uso del acento': orthographic accent normally not written; to distinguish words differing only in stress ('acento (o acento tonal)') accents falling on antepenultimate syllables are written on headwords; 'Si no se escribe, el acento cae en la penúltima sílaba'; prosodic stress varies in many words; stress unpredictable in onomatopoeic words (examples pánkotsi, tinti, punatagantsi). Apuntes gramaticales 7.1 p.875: descriptive particles vary in stress/length/intonation by context. Refers to Snell 1974 and Solís 1973 for phonology.

Atalaya: Universidad Católica Sedes Sapientiae – Nopoki. 326 pp. (archive.org item guia-teorica-matsigenka-2020)
sources.note: Pedagogical (native-speaker authors), pp.224-226 'El acento en el idioma matsigenka' (fn. cites Aza 1923 pp.61-62): no tilde used; no final-stressed words or monosyllables except onomatopoeia; antepenult stress very frequent — when the penult vowel is weak (e,i) and the antepenult strong (a,o,u) (impókiro, mániro, magátiro), in imperatives (kánteri, névite), verb forms with pronominal affixes (nonkamánteri, ipákena), words in -rika/-mera/-rira (ogatsantsárika), many reflexives in -empa (mánempa, kishítempa); some -empa reflexives are penult-stressed (sekatémpa, kaatémpa, kaentémpa).

sources.citation: Snell, Betty. 2008 [1998]. Pequeño diccionario machiguenga-castellano. Documento de Trabajo 32. Lima: ILV. 412 pp. (archive.org item machiguenguadiccionario, scanned text + PDF)
sources.note: p.14 'El uso del acento': same convention as 2011 — accents written only when on the antepenult (pánkotsi, kíraari, árakintsi); not written on words whose stress falls on the penult (punatagantsi, mantsigarintsi, tinti).

sources.note: Describes NANTI (nant1250) stress, sec. 6.2.3.1 pp.231-235: left-to-right disyllabic iambs, rightmost primary stress, verbal stress sonority-sensitive (a > e,o,u > i), nominal stress quality-insensitive with lexical stress (after Crowhurst & Michael 2005).
